APX-000007.transcript:
Customer (Susan Martin): Why did my equalized payment change again? Nobody told me this was happening.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Hi Susan Martin, Sipho Nkosi here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Susan Martin): If the point of this plan is predictable payments, why does it keep moving?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Thanks for bearing with us on this. Let me go through the bill with you properly.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Susan Martin): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Susan Martin): This is the third time this year my equalized amount has changed on me.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): When did you first join the equalization plan?
Customer (Susan Martin): About two years ago, when we moved in.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Did you get a notice before the amount changed?
Customer (Susan Martin): No. I found out when the payment came out.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Has anything changed at home, like a new appliance or more people?
Customer (Susan Martin): We had a baby, so the heat's been on more.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Let me take a look. I've reviewed the equalization plan's 12-month usage average and the reconciliation adjustment that triggered the change.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): The plan averages your last twelve months of usage and is reviewed at month six. If usage runs higher than the estimate, the difference is added.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Your usage this year is running above last year's, which is why the amount went up.
Customer (Susan Martin): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): The equalization amount is recalculated from your usage history under the plan terms, and I can't reverse an adjustment that's already been applied — what I can do is flag your file so the next change comes with a heads-up call before it hits your bill.
Customer (Susan Martin): So the CA$600 is still due?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): The adjustment has been applied and I can't reverse it. I can split it over two payments instead of one.
Customer (Susan Martin): And next time?
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): I've flagged your file so the next change comes with a call before it reaches your bill.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): To recap: the adjustment stands, it can be split over two payments, and your file is flagged for a call before the next change.
Customer (Susan Martin): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Sipho Nkosi): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Agent Sipho Nkosi reviewed the equalization plan's 12-month usage average and the reconciliation adjustment that triggered the change. APX-000048.transcript:
Customer (Susan Reid): This bill says 'estimated read' again. Can someone come and read my meter?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Hi Susan Reid, Nomsa Khumalo here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Susan Reid): If the estimate is wrong, how does the correction actually happen on a future bill?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Understood. Let me pull up the account and look at the charges before I say anything.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Susan Reid): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Susan Reid): Is there a way I can submit my own meter reading instead of waiting?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Do you have a reading from the meter today?
Customer (Susan Reid): I took a photo this morning. It's much lower than the bill.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): How many estimated bills have you had in a row?
Customer (Susan Reid): Three, I think.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Would a self-read reminder by email work for you?
Customer (Susan Reid): Yes, if it actually gets used.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Let me take a look. I've checked the meter-read schedule for the account and confirmed whether a self-read or field read was available.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): When our reader can't reach the meter, the bill is estimated from your past usage for the same months.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): I've scheduled an actual field read for your next cycle and shown you how to submit a self-read online in the meantime, so this month's estimate will be corrected against the real number once it's read.
Customer (Susan Reid): So I'll get the overcharge back?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): It's credited automatically on the next bill once the actual read is in.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): To recap: your self-read is on file, the next bill corrects the estimate, and the reader will call ahead about the gate.
Customer (Susan Reid): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

APX-000098.transcript:
Customer (Emily Thompson): I'm moving next week and need gas stopped at my old place and started at the new one.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Hi Emily Thompson, Nomsa Khumalo here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Emily Thompson): What's the actual turnaround time between the stop and the start?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): No problem, I can help with that.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Emily Thompson): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Emily Thompson): Do I need to be home for anyone to come out, or can this be done remotely?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): What date do you need the stop to take effect?
Customer (Emily Thompson): The last day of the month. That's when we hand the keys back.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Is the new address in one of our service areas?
Customer (Emily Thompson): Yes, it's still in Leduc County.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Is the email on your account still current, for the confirmations?
Customer (Emily Thompson): It's an old one. Can you change it to my new email?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Let me take a look. I've processed the account request and confirmed the effective date against the service address change.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): A stop and start on the same day is routine. We read the old meter on the move-out date so you only pay to that day.
Customer (Emily Thompson): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): I've got the stop set for your move-out date and the start scheduled for your new address the same day, no technician visit needed for a standard meter transfer, and I've sent both confirmations to your email.
Customer (Emily Thompson): And the final bill for the old place?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): It comes within two weeks of the move-out read.
Customer (Emily Thompson): Will the new account use the same payment details?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Yes, the pre-authorized payment moves over with you.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): To recap, everything's noted on your file, and the team will follow up with you.
Customer (Emily Thompson): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

APX-000109.transcript:
Customer (Chris Grant): My bill jumped and I don't understand why. Did something change with my rate?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Hi Chris Grant, Zanele Radebe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Chris Grant): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Good question, a lot of customers are asking about this one. Let me check your account.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Chris Grant): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Chris Grant): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Is this a home, a farm, or a business account?
Customer (Chris Grant): It's our home. We're not a business.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?
Customer (Chris Grant): By mail, a couple of weeks ago.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Do you have any irrigation or shop meters on the same account?
Customer (Chris Grant): No, just the house.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Let me take a look. I've pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Since August 1, Rate 1 covers accounts using under 4,000 GJ a year and Rate 2 covers larger users. The AUC approved it as Phase 2 of the rate restructuring.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Your usage puts you right at the edge of the new Rate 2 threshold, so this bill reflects the higher rate class — I don't have authority to move you back to Rate 1 manually, that's set by your metered usage under the AUC-approved structure.
Customer (Chris Grant): Can't you just put me back on Rate 1?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Not manually. The class follows your metered usage under the approved structure.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): To recap: your usage puts you in Rate 2 for now, the class is reviewed against annual usage, and the details are in your email.
Customer (Chris Grant): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.
APX-000109.narrative_summary: Chris Grant, an Apex Utilities customer, contacted support on a rate-class change case. Agent Zanele Radebe pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account. Customer (Tyler Stewart): Our furnace takes a few seconds to light after the fan starts. Is that a problem?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Hi Tyler Stewart, Sipho van der Merwe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Tyler Stewart): Is this something I should be worried about, or is it normal?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Happy to help with that.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Tyler Stewart): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Tyler Stewart): Should I have someone look at it, or is it fine to keep using?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Do you smell gas at all right now?
Customer (Tyler Stewart): No, nothing like that.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): How old is the furnace?
Customer (Tyler Stewart): About fifteen years.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): When was it last serviced by a licensed technician?
Customer (Tyler Stewart): A couple of years ago, I think.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Let me take a look. I've walked through the standard non-emergency safety guidance and checked for any signs that needed a field visit.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): A few clicks or a soft whoosh before the burner lights is the igniter and the gas catching. That's normal on most furnaces.
Customer (Tyler Stewart): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): What you're describing is the normal ignition sequence, so there's nothing to worry about. If the sound changes, or you ever smell gas, call us straight away.
Customer (Tyler Stewart): So I don't need anything from Apex?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Not for this. A yearly service by a licensed technician is still a good idea at fifteen years.
Customer (Tyler Stewart): And if I ever do smell gas?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Leave the house and call our 24-hour emergency line from outside.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): To recap: the ignition sound is normal, a yearly service is worth booking, and the emergency line is there if you ever smell gas.
Customer (Tyler Stewart): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (Jennifer Ross): I signed up for budget billing so my payments would be predictable, and now I've got a CA$600 catch-up bill.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Hi Jennifer Ross, Karabo Zulu here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Jennifer Ross): If the point of this plan is predictable payments, why does it keep moving?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Thanks for bearing with us on this. Let me go through the bill with you properly.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Jennifer Ross): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Jennifer Ross): This is the third time this year my equalized amount has changed on me.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): When did you first join the equalization plan?
Customer (Jennifer Ross): About two years ago, when we moved in.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Did you get a notice before the amount changed?
Customer (Jennifer Ross): No. I found out when the payment came out.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Would you rather stay on the plan or go back to regular billing?
Customer (Jennifer Ross): Stay on it, if it stops jumping around.

Agent (Karabo Zulu): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): The plan averages your last twelve months of usage and is reviewed at month six. If usage runs higher than the estimate, the difference is added.
Customer (Jennifer Ross): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): The equalization amount is recalculated from your usage history under the plan terms, and I can't reverse an adjustment that's already been applied — what I can do is flag your file so the next change comes with a heads-up call before it hits your bill.
Customer (Jennifer Ross): So the CA$600 is still due?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): The adjustment has been applied and I can't reverse it. I can split it over two payments instead of one.
Customer (Jennifer Ross): And next time?
Agent (Karabo Zulu): I've flagged your file so the next change comes with a call before it reaches your bill.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): To recap: the adjustment stands, it can be split over two payments, and your file is flagged for a call before the next change.
Customer (Jennifer Ross): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Karabo Zulu): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

APX-000268.transcript:
Customer (Karen Campbell): My bill jumped and I don't understand why. Did something change with my rate?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Hi Karen Campbell, Vusi Molefe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Karen Campbell): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Happy to explain it. Let me pull up your usage first.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Karen Campbell): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Karen Campbell): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Roughly how much gas do you use in a year, or should I look it up?
Customer (Karen Campbell): No idea. Can you look it up?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?
Customer (Karen Campbell): By mail, a couple of weeks ago.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Let me take a look. I've pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Since August 1, Rate 1 covers accounts using under 4,000 GJ a year and Rate 2 covers larger users. The AUC approved it as Phase 2 of the rate restructuring.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): You're on Rate 1 since your annual usage is under 4,000 GJ, so the main change is the way the distribution charge is broken out on the bill — your total shouldn't move much. I've sent the AUC decision summary to your email so you have it on file.
Customer (Karen Campbell): So my total won't go up much?
Agent (Vusi Molefe): It shouldn't. Most of this month's jump is colder weather, not the rate change.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): To recap: you're staying on Rate 1, the change is mostly how the bill is laid out, and the summary is in your email.
Customer (Karen Campbell): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Vusi Molefe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

APX-000371.transcript:
Customer (Robert Kerr): I got a letter about a 'Rate 1' and 'Rate 2' change and I have no idea what it means for my bill.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Hi Robert Kerr, Naledi Nkosi here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Robert Kerr): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Good question, a lot of customers are asking about this one. Let me check your account.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Robert Kerr): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Robert Kerr): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Roughly how much gas do you use in a year, or should I look it up?
Customer (Robert Kerr): No idea. Can you look it up?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?
Customer (Robert Kerr): By mail, a couple of weeks ago.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Do you have any irrigation or shop meters on the same account?
Customer (Robert Kerr): No, just the house.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Let me take a look. I've pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Since August 1, Rate 1 covers accounts using under 4,000 GJ a year and Rate 2 covers larger users. The AUC approved it as Phase 2 of the rate restructuring.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Your annual usage is well under that, so you stay on Rate 1. What changed is how the distribution charge is shown on the bill.
Customer (Robert Kerr): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): You're on Rate 1 since your annual usage is under 4,000 GJ, so the main change is the way the distribution charge is broken out on the bill — your total shouldn't move much. I've sent the AUC decision summary to your email so you have it on file.
Customer (Robert Kerr): So my total won't go up much?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): It shouldn't. Most of this month's jump is colder weather, not the rate change.
Customer (Robert Kerr): Can I get that in writing?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): The AUC summary and your usage figure are in your email now.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): To recap: you're staying on Rate 1, the change is mostly how the bill is laid out, and the summary is in your email.
Customer (Robert Kerr): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (Brian Scott): My bill jumped and I don't understand why. Did something change with my rate?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Hi Brian Scott, Lerato Ndlovu here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Brian Scott): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?

Customer (Brian Scott): So my total won't go up much?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): It shouldn't. Most of this month's jump is colder weather, not the rate change.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): To recap: you're staying on Rate 1, the change is mostly how the bill is laid out, and the summary is in your email.
Customer (Brian Scott): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (Nicole Grant): I'm looking at a distribution charge on a property that used zero gas this month.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Hi Nicole Grant, Vusi Jacobs here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Nicole Grant): This isn't the first time — I feel like I'm being charged fees just for having an account.

Customer (Nicole Grant): Can you actually break down where every line item on this bill comes from?

Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Is the property occupied at the moment?

Customer (Nicole Grant): That's not really the answer I was hoping for, but okay.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): I've logged everything here so if this comes up again, the next agent has the full picture.

APX-000696.transcript:
Customer (Michael Douglas): I'm following up again — why did my equalized payment change again? Nobody told me this was happening.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Hi Michael Douglas, Vusi Jacobs here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Michael Douglas): I already explained this on my last contact.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): I'm sorry about that — let me look at what happened last time and pick up from there.
Customer (Michael Douglas): This is the third time this year my equalized amount has changed on me.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Understood. Let me pull up the account and look at the charges before I say anything.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Michael Douglas): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Michael Douglas): If the point of this plan is predictable payments, why does it keep moving?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): When did you first join the equalization plan?
Customer (Michael Douglas): About two years ago, when we moved in.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Did you get a notice before the amount changed?
Customer (Michael Douglas): No. I found out when the payment came out.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Let me take a look. I've reviewed the equalization plan's 12-month usage average and the reconciliation adjustment that triggered the change.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): The plan averages your last twelve months of usage and is reviewed at month six. If usage runs higher than the estimate, the difference is added.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): The equalization amount is recalculated from your usage history under the plan terms, and I can't reverse an adjustment that's already been applied — what I can do is flag your file so the next change comes with a heads-up call before it hits your bill.
Customer (Michael Douglas): So the CA$600 is still due?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): The adjustment has been applied and I can't reverse it. I can split it over two payments instead of one.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): To recap: the adjustment stands, it can be split over two payments, and your file is flagged for a call before the next change.
Customer (Michael Douglas): That's not really the answer I was hoping for, but okay.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): I've logged everything here so if this comes up again, the next agent has the full picture.

APX-000699.transcript:
Customer (Chris Martin): I'm following up again — you charged me far more in fees than the gas actually cost. That can't be right.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Hi Chris Martin, Sipho van der Merwe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Chris Martin): I already explained this on my last contact.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): I'm sorry about that — let me look at what happened last time and pick up from there.
Customer (Chris Martin): This isn't the first time — I feel like I'm being charged fees just for having an account.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Understood. Let me pull up the account and look at the charges before I say anything.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Chris Martin): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Chris Martin): Can you actually break down where every line item on this bill comes from?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Have you raised this with us before?
Customer (Chris Martin): Once before, and I was told it's just how the bill works.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Would a line-by-line breakdown by email help?
Customer (Chris Martin): Yes, I want to see where every dollar comes from.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Let me take a look. I've reviewed the itemized charges line by line against metered usage and the current distribution rate schedule.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): The distribution charge and the fixed daily charge are set by the AUC for your rate class, so they apply even when the meter reads zero.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): The distribution and fixed charges you're seeing are billed under the AUC-approved rate schedule regardless of how much gas you actually use that month — I can explain the structure, but I don't have the authority to waive a regulated charge.
Customer (Chris Martin): So there's nothing you can do?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): I can't waive a regulated charge. I can send the dispute to a billing specialist so every line is checked, not just explained.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): To recap: the regulated charges stand, a billing specialist is checking each line, and you'll hear back within five business days.
Customer (Chris Martin): That's not really the answer I was hoping for, but okay.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): I've logged everything here so if this comes up again, the next agent has the full picture.

Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): To recap: the adjustment stands, it can be split over two payments, and your file is flagged for a call before the next change.
